prompt: A caller wants a first visit with Dr. Alvarez next week after a fall that left the knee swollen. What should the CMAA collect before offering a time?

options.text: Legal name, birth date, insurance, and the reason for the visit so the slot length can be set
Legal name and the insurance card, with the reason left for the provider to discover in the room
The insurance plan plus a prepaid deposit, saving the legal name and birth date for the arrival desk
Legal name, insurance, and a diagnosis code picked now so the correct visit type can be chosen

explanation: The booking call has to support eligibility, reminders, and the right slot length. The CMAA records who the patient is, how the visit will be paid, and why they are coming, then uses that reason to choose the provider time from the matrix. Choosing a diagnosis code is the provider's step after the encounter.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a partial registration with a finished booking; without the reason, slot length and visit type are guesses.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the scheduling call with arrival paperwork; name and birth date are needed now for an eligibility check, and a deposit does not create the visit.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the CMAA with a coder; a diagnosis code comes from the provider's note after the encounter, not from the booking call.

prompt: Dr. Chen blocks Tuesday mornings for hospital rounds and wants complete physicals kept in the early afternoon. What does the scheduling matrix let the CMAA set before any patient is booked?

options.text: A log of each arrival and departure time that feeds the daily patient-flow sheet
Blocks for hospital rounds and other hours when the provider or the office is unavailable
Today's already-booked names with chart numbers, printed so those charts can be pulled
A running tally of no-shows and late cancels used to post a missed-visit charge

explanation: The scheduling matrix is set before any patient is booked. It blocks time the provider is unavailable, such as hospital rounds, meetings, and hours the office is closed, so a name cannot be placed there. Reserving the early afternoon for physicals is a visit-type template, not that unavailable-time grid.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the scheduling matrix with a patient-tracking log; the matrix is built in advance to hold or release time.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the matrix with the daily appointment list; the list is printed after people are booked, while the matrix exists before that.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the matrix with the no-show log; missed visits are documented under the no-show policy, not by blocking unavailable time.

prompt: The office manager asks when it is reasonable to put two patients into overlapping times on purpose. Which situation fits a planned double-book?

options.text: The day is full and a new patient wants the next complete physical squeezed into a gap
Both patients need a long procedure that depends on the same exam room and equipment
Both visits are brief, and the overlap fits the way this provider already works
The provider is running behind, so every remaining appointment on the day gets shortened

explanation: Double-booking is a planned overlap for short visits the provider can absorb, not a way to force long visits into a full day. It works when it matches that provider's workflow. It is a poor fix for a provider who is already running behind.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a short double-book with squeezing a long new-patient physical into a day that has no full slot left.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a workable overlap with two long procedures that need the same room, which stacks delay instead of saving time.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses planned double-booking with compressing the rest of the day because the provider is behind.

prompt: Mr. Patel arrives eighteen minutes after his diabetes follow-up, and two other patients are already waiting for their own times. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Move Mr. Patel ahead of the patients who came on time so that his personal delay stays short
Cancel the visit immediately and rebook him, using the same step for a short delay or a long one
Check him in without an explanation and leave him until some later gap opens up in the day
Follow the written late policy, either working him in or rebooking him

explanation: Late arrival is handled by the office's written policy, which may work the patient in or rebook them. The aim is to protect patients who arrived on time and any visit that cannot be delayed, while still telling the late patient the real options.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses fairness with favoring the late patient; moving ahead of on-time patients spreads one delay to people who came as scheduled.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a written late policy with an automatic cancel for every delay, including ones the policy would still work in.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses check-in with service; the patient should hear the expected wait or the rebook option the policy allows.

prompt: A cardiology referral is required by the health plan, and the patient wants a date next month. What should the CMAA confirm before that date is set?

options.text: The referral or authorization number, and whether that cardiologist is in the plan network
The copay printed on the card, plus the cardiologist's office hours and street address
The referring provider's NPI, plus which weekdays the patient prefers to make the trip
The cardiologist's fee list, plus how much of the yearly deductible the patient has already met

explanation: A specialist visit the plan calls a referral needs an authorization or referral number and an in-network specialist before the date is locked. Copays, NPIs, and fee lists do not replace that check, and a missing authorization is a common denial.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses benefit details and driving directions with the authorization number and network status that prevent a denied referral.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses claim identifiers and scheduling preferences with the plan's referral and network requirements.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a cost estimate with the referral check; a fee list does not prove the visit is authorized or in network.

prompt: Four established patients are marked for 9:00 and will be seen in the order they walk in. Which scheduling method is the office using?

options.text: Stream scheduling, with one patient locked to each separate clock time across the morning grid
Wave scheduling, with several patients sharing the hour and seen in arrival order
Cluster scheduling, with one visit type such as physicals filling that whole morning block
Open-hours scheduling, with people seen as they arrive and no appointment written on the book

explanation: Wave scheduling books several patients to the same hour and then sees them in arrival order. It is different from a single fixed time for each person, from grouping one kind of visit, and from a walk-in block with no names.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses wave scheduling with stream scheduling, which gives each patient a separate clock time.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses wave scheduling with cluster scheduling, which groups one visit type into a block.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses wave scheduling with open hours, which has no names booked to a time.

prompt: After the visit the provider checks the exam and the diagnoses on a form the front desk uses to enter charges. What is that form meant to do?

options.text: Stand in for the progress note as the legal record of what happened during the visit
Request prior authorization from the health plan before any service listed on it is performed
Capture the services and diagnoses from this visit so the charges can be entered
Show the balance the patient still owes once the health plan has paid its share of the claim

explanation: The encounter form, often called a superbill, is the charge-capture sheet for that visit. The provider marks services and diagnoses, and the front desk uses it to enter charges. The progress note remains the legal record, and the patient statement comes later.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the encounter form with the legal medical record; the progress note still has to support every charge.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the encounter form with a prior-authorization request, which is sent before the service, not filled in after it.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the encounter form with the patient statement, which is produced later from posted payments.

prompt: Someone calls the front desk about chest pain that started an hour ago and now comes with sweating. The emergency script is at the desk. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Offer the next routine opening about three months out and advise the caller to rest at home until that date
Treat the pain as heartburn and book a non-urgent visit with the provider for some time next week
End the call, because front-desk staff are not expected to act on symptom calls of this kind
Follow the emergency script, send the caller to 911, and alert clinical staff

explanation: Chest pain with sweating is handled by the office emergency script, not by a front-desk diagnosis or a routine future slot. The CMAA directs the caller to 911 and alerts clinical staff immediately. Administrative staff do not decide the cause.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an emergency script with routine booking; chest pain with sweating is not a visit to park months out.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses administrative protocol with diagnosing; the CMAA does not decide the pain is heartburn.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a non-clinical role with hanging up; the front desk still follows the emergency script and alerts clinical staff.

prompt: During registration a new patient asks what happens if a future visit is missed. The practice has a written no-show rule. How should that rule be handled?

options.text: Explain it before it is needed, document that sharing, and apply it the same way each time
Let each receptionist waive it for familiar patients and enforce it on people they do not know well
Say nothing until a visit is missed, then describe the rule while the patient is already upset
Keep it in the staff manual and leave it off patient forms so the front desk avoids an argument

explanation: A no-show rule works when patients hear it before they miss, the conversation or form is documented, and every patient is treated under the same rule. A manual that patients have not seen, or a rule introduced after the miss, is hard to enforce fairly.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a written policy with personal discretion; waiving it for familiar patients is uneven enforcement.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses advance notice with a surprise after the miss; patients need the rule before it is applied.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an internal manual with a patient policy; a rule patients have not been shown cannot be fairly enforced.

prompt: Thursday morning is reserved for school physicals and Thursday afternoon for suture checks so the same supplies can stay out. What scheduling pattern is that?

options.text: Wave scheduling, because several patients are told to arrive together at the top of each hour
Cluster scheduling, because similar visits are grouped so one setup can be reused
Open booking, because unscheduled hours are stacked at the beginning and the end of the clinic day
Payer batching, because patients are grouped by insurance plan so their claims can go out together

explanation: Cluster scheduling groups similar appointments, such as physicals or suture checks, into a block so rooms, supplies, and staff stay set up. It is not several unrelated patients sharing the top of an hour, and it is not a walk-in period.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses cluster scheduling with wave scheduling, which stacks several patients at one arrival time.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses cluster scheduling with open hours; a walk-in block is not a group of like appointments.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses visit-type grouping with batching claims by payer, which is a billing task rather than a schedule design.

prompt: Idle gaps bother the provider, so the manager moves the morning to several arrivals at each hour. What is that change meant to accomplish?

options.text: Give every patient a separate slot spaced evenly so the waiting time stays very small
Book several patients for one shared arrival time so the provider is not left idle
Group matching visit types into blocks so rooms and equipment can be prepared together
Drop set appointment times and see whoever walks in during the posted hours of the clinic

explanation: Wave scheduling is used to cut idle provider time by having several patients arrive at one hour, then seeing them in arrival order. It still uses booked times. It does not space single patients evenly, and it does not group the day by visit type.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses wave scheduling with stream scheduling, where each person has a separate evenly spaced time.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a shared arrival time with cluster scheduling, which organizes the day by visit type.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses wave scheduling with open hours; wave still assigns patients to a specific hour.

prompt: Before tomorrow's physical, the CMAA sees a health plan this office has not billed during the past year. What should be confirmed with that payer?

options.text: That a card copy and a photo ID are scanned, which together prove the coverage is active today
That coverage is active, which services it includes, and whether a referral is required
Active coverage alone, because any authorization is the specialist office's duty to obtain later
The copay amount and this office's fee for a physical, which together are enough to close the claim

explanation: Verification with the payer should show that coverage is active, what the plan actually covers, and whether this visit needs a referral or authorization. A card on file does not prove eligibility, and a copay figure alone does not either.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses identity documents with eligibility; a card copy does not prove the plan is active today.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a full benefit check with eligibility alone; skipping referral rules is a common reason for a denial.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one copay figure with verification; the copay does not show whether coverage is active or an authorization is required.

prompt: A receptionist wants a neighbor's missed visit overlooked and the same step enforced on every other patient. Which approach holds up?

options.text: Decide each case from the patient's personal history so regular visitors receive more leeway
State the rule in advance, apply it the same way to everyone, and record each miss
Post the rule at the desk but use it for first-time patients and skip it for people already known
Remove the patient from the practice the first time one appointment is missed without a call

explanation: The policy holds up when it is stated in advance, used the same way for every patient, and written in the record when a visit is missed. Favoring a neighbor, limiting it to new patients, or ending care after one miss breaks that standard.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses consistent policy with case-by-case favors; uneven enforcement is hard to defend and feels unfair.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a practice-wide rule with a new-patient-only rule; established patients are covered by the same policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one missed visit with grounds for discharge; a sound policy records the miss and warns before the relationship ends.

prompt: Registration is opening a chart for someone who has never been seen in this office. Which details belong in the demographic record?

options.text: Legal name, date of birth, sex, home address, and the phone number on file
A nickname, date of birth, and an emergency contact, with the health plan added later at billing
Legal name, a Social Security number, and the employer name used as the main identifiers
Legal name, today's main complaint, and drug allergies typed into the chart by the front desk

explanation: The demographic record identifies the person: legal name, date of birth, sex, address, and phone. Insurance member identifiers are checked on the coverage record, which is a separate registration step. A nickname does not replace the legal name, a Social Security number is not the core identifier, and allergies belong in the clinical intake.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a nickname with the legal name, and it postpones insurance identifiers that are needed before the visit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a Social Security number and the employer with the core demographic fields; legal name, birth date, and contact information identify the person.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the demographic record with the clinical intake; allergies and the complaint are not the registration identifiers.

prompt: If two patients arrive claiming the same appointment slot, the CMAA should

options.text: Seat whichever patient checked in first and ask the other to rebook
Review the schedule/documentation and escalate per office protocol
Have both patients wait while the provider decides who will be seen first
Apologize and see both by shortening each visit to fit into the one slot

explanation: De-escalate, verify records, and follow protocol; protect privacy while resolving errors. The goal is to resolve the conflict without blaming either patient.

distractorExplanations.a: First to check in ignores the actual booking record; the CMAA should verify the schedule before deciding who keeps the slot.
distractorExplanations.c: Schedule conflicts are an administrative task; the CMAA verifies the record and escalates to the office manager, not the treating provider.
distractorExplanations.d: Halving two visits to fit one slot compromises care for both patients; the conflict should be resolved by reviewing the schedule.

prompt: Two people are placed at the top of each hour, then one person twenty minutes later and one person twenty minutes after that. What is this pattern called?

options.text: Modified wave, with a pair at the hour and single visits staggered afterward
Pure wave, with every patient in that hour told to arrive at the same minute on the clock
Cluster booking, with a single kind of visit filling the entire afternoon on this template
Double-booking, with two long procedures forced to share one exam room at the same moment

explanation: Modified wave starts the hour with more than one patient and then staggers the rest, which softens the wait of a pure wave. A pattern of two at the hour and singles afterward is that method. It is not defined by visit type or by two long procedures in one room.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses modified wave with pure wave; pure wave seats the whole hour at one minute, not in a staggered pattern.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses modified wave with cluster scheduling, which is defined by visit type rather than by staggered clock times.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses modified wave with double-booking two long procedures into one room.

prompt: At checkout the provider asks for a blood-pressure visit in six weeks, and the patient is ready to leave the desk. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Book a return time before the patient leaves and place it on the schedule
Ask the patient to call back sometime during those six weeks when a day feels convenient
Leave the booking for a nurse to do later from the note, without giving the patient a time today
Enter a chart reminder and wait for the patient to call before any real appointment is created

explanation: When the provider asks for a return visit, the CMAA offers a real time before the patient leaves. That checkout step is more reliable than a vague invitation to call back or a chart note that still depends on the patient calling later.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses checkout booking with a vague callback; the return the provider requested is most reliable when it is placed before the patient leaves.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the CMAA's scheduling duty with a later nursing task; the patient is at the desk and can leave with a real time.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a chart tickler with the appointment itself; a reminder that waits on a later phone call often fails to become a visit.

prompt: Two patients share a last name, and both are in the waiting room for afternoon visits. How should the CMAA confirm who is checking in for the 2:15?

options.text: Ask for two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, before opening a chart
Call the last name into the room and hand the chart to whichever person stands up first
Match the face to an old identification photo and skip questions so the check-in line keeps moving
Rely on the insurance card alone, because the member number can select the correct chart by itself

explanation: Check-in uses two identifiers, commonly full name and date of birth, before a chart is opened. Calling out a shared last name, trusting an old photo, or relying on one insurance card can attach the visit to the wrong person.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a last-name call-out with identification; two people can answer, and the wrong chart can be opened.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a glance at an old photo with two identifiers; appearance is not a reliable check-in match.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a single insurance card with two-identifier check-in; the card can belong to the wrong family member.

prompt: A booked physical cancels at noon, and three patients asked earlier this week to be seen sooner. What should the CMAA do with the opening?

options.text: Call the cancellation list in list order and book the first person who can come
Leave the hour empty so the provider can rest, even though those patients asked to come in sooner
Give the hour to a staff member's relative who would like a physical on the same day
Post the open time on the public website and accept the first unfamiliar caller who replies

explanation: A same-day opening from a cancellation is offered through the cancellation list, in the order the office keeps, to the first person who can come. That protects access. It is not a staff perk and not a slot to advertise while known patients are waiting.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a patient cancellation with a provider break; the opening was a booked slot, and people already asked to be seen sooner.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the cancellation list with staff convenience; relatives should not jump ahead of patients who asked for the time.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a managed cancellation list with a public posting; the office fills the opening from the patients who already asked.

prompt: The orthopedic office will not schedule until it has the imaging report and the referring note. The authorization number is already on file. What should the CMAA send?

options.text: The imaging report, the referring note, the authorization number, and patient demographics
The authorization number by itself, leaving the clinical papers for the specialist to chase later
The entire chart for every prior year, including visits unrelated to this orthopedic referral
A diagnosis code the CMAA selects from the complaint so the orthopedic office has something to bill

explanation: The receiving office set the contents: the imaging report, the referring note, plus the authorization number and demographics needed to book. The CMAA sends that packet. The CMAA does not invent a diagnosis, and unrelated chart years are not part of this request.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an authorization number with the whole referral packet; the receiving office said it will not book without the imaging and the note.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a focused referral packet with the entire old chart; unrelated years are not what the orthopedic office asked to receive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses referral paperwork with coding; the CMAA does not invent a diagnosis code so another office can bill.

prompt: Dr. Nguyen is ill and calls at 7:30 in the morning with a full schedule of booked patients. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Keep every patient scheduled and have them wait in the office in case Dr. Nguyen feels well enough later
Notify the affected patients, block the slots the provider will miss, and rebook or move them if policy allows
Erase the appointments and let patients discover the closure when they arrive at the front door
Ask the medical assistant to see the morning patients so the original appointment times can stay in place

explanation: A provider who calls out ill needs the missed time blocked and those patients told before they arrive. Each person is rebooked or, when office policy allows, offered another authorized provider. Patients should not wait on a possible recovery, and a medical assistant does not take over the physician's schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses hope of a quick recovery with a plan; patients who already hold a time should not be left waiting on the chance the provider rallies.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a quiet deletion with notice; patients who still hold a time need a call, not a surprise at the door.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a medical assistant with a substitute physician; another person sees those patients only when the office has authorized that provider.

prompt: Visits on this template start fifteen minutes apart, and the provider expects one person in the exam room at a time. Which appointment method is this?

options.text: Wave scheduling, because several people are instructed to arrive together at the top of each hour
Modified wave, because a pair arrives on the hour and later visits are staggered through the rest of it
Stream scheduling, because each patient is given one fixed interval and is seen at that time
Open hours, because patients may walk in at any point while the office door stays unlocked for the day

explanation: Stream, or time-specified, scheduling gives each patient one fixed interval and expects one person at a time. Even spacing is the point. It is not a shared top-of-hour arrival and not a walk-in block.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses stream scheduling with wave scheduling, which brings several patients to the top of the hour.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses stream scheduling with modified wave, which starts the hour with a pair and then staggers singles.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a fixed-interval template with open hours, which does not give each person a start time.

prompt: Next Tuesday's physical includes a fasting lipid panel, and the patient is booking the visit by phone today. What should the CMAA pass along?

options.text: Skip any food instruction, because the drawing station explains preparation on the morning of the test
Promise that the panel will look normal if breakfast is skipped on that single morning before the draw
Give the fasting instruction and the arrival time, and note the draw on the appointment
Tell the patient to stop every home medication tonight so the laboratory result is easier for the provider to read

explanation: Preparation that is already on the order, such as fasting for this lipid panel, is given when the visit is booked, and the appointment is flagged so the team expects the draw. The CMAA does not promise a normal result and does not tell the patient to stop medicines.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses booking-time instructions with a morning-of lab speech; the order is already a fasting panel, so the patient needs that before arriving.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a prep instruction with a promise about the result; the CMAA cannot tell the patient the panel will be normal.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses fasting with a medication hold; stopping home drugs is a provider order, not a front-desk instruction.

prompt: One caller needs a first complete physical, and another established patient needs a brief medication-refill visit the same morning. How should the lengths be booked?

options.text: Use the same brief slot for both, because a complete physical and a refill take about the same time
Give the refill the long slot and the physical the short one, since a new patient usually moves faster
Use the matrix's longer block for the new physical and the short slot for the refill
Decline the physical until that caller has already been seen once in a short get-acquainted visit

explanation: The matrix assigns a longer block to a first complete physical and a short block to a brief established visit such as a medication refill. Booking them as if they take the same time, or reversing the lengths, misuses the template.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses two visit types that the matrix times differently; a first physical is not a brief refill.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses which visit needs the long block; the new complete physical is the longer one, not the refill.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a first physical with a visit that must be earned by an earlier short appointment.

prompt: Mandarin interpretation is required for a forty-minute new-patient visit, and the office uses a phone interpreter service. What should the CMAA arrange?

options.text: Ask a bilingual patient in the waiting room to interpret so the visit can stay inside a short slot
Keep the usual short slot and ask the provider to speak more slowly throughout the encounter
Hold extra minutes on the schedule and confirm the interpreter line before the patient arrives
Tell the patient to bring a child who speaks English so the appointment template does not need a change

explanation: Language access is arranged before the visit: extra time on the schedule and a confirmed interpreter service. Another patient, slower English, or a child is not a qualified interpreter and can harm privacy or accuracy.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a qualified interpreter with another patient; that invites a privacy breach and an unreliable translation.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses language access with speaking slowly; a short slot and slower English do not replace an interpreter.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a qualified interpreter with a child; minors should not carry the clinical conversation.

prompt: Dermatology access expires at the end of this month under the plan, but the patient wants a date about six weeks away. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Book the date six weeks out and assume the plan will honor the referral number after the end date
Tell the patient a referral number remains usable on any later date once the plan has issued it
Explain the end date, offer a time inside the window, or request a renewal
Drop the referral and tell the patient to see dermatology without an update to the health plan

explanation: A referral is usable through the end date the plan set. The CMAA states that date, offers a time inside the window, or asks for a renewal before booking past it. Assuming the old number will still pay, or dropping the referral, leads to a denial.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an active referral with one past its end date; booking beyond the window and hoping the plan pays invites a denial.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses issuance of a number with open-ended validity; the plan set an end date, and that date controls the booking.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses renewal with dropping the referral; the patient still needs a valid authorization or a date inside the current window.

prompt: Friday morning has no names on the schedule from eight to ten, and acute patients are seen in the order they arrive. What is that block called?

options.text: Wave scheduling, because several names are written down to arrive together at the top of the hour
Cluster scheduling, because Friday morning is being held as a block of similar school physicals
Stream scheduling, because each arriving person still receives a private fifteen-minute start time
Open-hours scheduling, because patients come during a set block with no booked names

explanation: Open-hours scheduling holds a block of time with no names and sees patients in arrival order. Wave scheduling still books names to a clock time. Cluster scheduling groups a visit type. Stream scheduling assigns private start times.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses open hours with wave scheduling; wave still writes names onto a shared clock time.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses open hours with cluster scheduling; this block is defined by walk-in arrival, not by grouping physicals.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses open hours with stream scheduling; stream gives each person a private start time, and this block has no names.

prompt: Eligibility shows a copay due for today's established visit, and office policy is to collect it when the patient arrives. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Skip collection, because payment is the biller's job once the health plan has finished the claim
Collect the full allowed charge for the visit in place of the copay amount shown on the screen
Waive the copay while the waiting room is crowded so the provider is not held up by the desk
Collect the copay shown for this visit, following the office policy for arrival

explanation: When eligibility shows a copay and the office policy is to collect it at arrival, the CMAA collects that copay. The copay is not the full allowed charge, and a busy lobby is not a reason to skip a policy the patient was expected to meet.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses arrival collection with the biller's later posting; the policy is to collect this copay when the patient arrives.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a copay with the full allowed charge; the patient owes the copay shown, not the office's whole fee.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a busy lobby with permission to waive the copay; the policy is the same when the room is full.

prompt: A parent reports a fever since last night in a child who is awake, drinking, and breathing comfortably, and asks to be seen today. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Decide this is a virus and tell the parent that a visit is unnecessary for this kind of fever
Send the child to the emergency department, treating a fever of this description as an emergency
Book a routine physical three weeks out, because same-day openings are reserved for patients new to the practice
Use the same-day script, offer an acute or buffer slot, and escalate if that script says to

explanation: The CMAA does not diagnose a fever and does not send every fever to the emergency department. A child who is awake, drinking, and breathing comfortably is offered a same-day acute or buffer slot under the office script, and is escalated when that script lists emergency signs.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the front desk with a clinician; the CMAA does not decide the fever is a virus or cancel the need to be seen.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses this stable picture with an emergency-department visit; the child is awake, drinking, and breathing comfortably, so the same-day script applies.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an acute same-day need with a routine physical booked weeks out.

prompt: An HMO member asks for a surgeon who is outside the plan network, while in-network surgeons have open times. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Book that surgeon and assure the member the plan will pay the same amount it pays for an in-network visit
Refuse the discussion, because network status is the coder's concern after the claim has been sent
End the request, because a non-network surgeon sits outside the plan, and do not offer another name
Explain the coverage risk, offer an in-network surgeon who has time, and document the choice

explanation: For an HMO, an out-of-network surgeon can mean a denial or a higher patient bill. The CMAA explains that risk, offers an in-network surgeon who has time, and documents what the member decides. Promising equal payment, or refusing to discuss the request, leaves the member uninformed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an out-of-network request with a promise of in-network payment; the CMAA cannot assure the plan will pay the same.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses scheduling counsel with coding; network status matters before the referral is booked, not after a claim is dropped in the queue.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a coverage limit with ending the conversation; the member still needs the risk explained and an in-network name offered.

prompt: A court clerk calls the front desk and asks which file the practice would produce as the official record of this patient's care.

options.text: The documentation of care designated for clinical, legal, and billing use
The entire electronic archive, including audit logs, unfinished drafts, and staff messages
The provider's private notepad kept outside the patient chart
The ledger of charges and payments for each visit

explanation: The legal health record is the documentation the organization designates as its official record of care. That set is what the practice relies on for later clinical decisions, billing support, and legal requests. Audit leftovers, a private notepad, and the payment ledger are not substitutes for it.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the legal health record with the whole electronic archive; audit logs, drafts, and staff messages are usually outside the designated record.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a private working notepad with the official chart; notes kept outside the designated record are not the legal health record.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the financial ledger with the legal health record; charges support billing but do not replace the clinical documentation of care.

prompt: A consulting cardiologist requests recent visit notes to treat the same patient, and the chart contains no separate authorization for that doctor.

options.text: Hold the notes until the patient signs a written authorization naming this cardiology consult
Disclose for treatment, payment, and operations without a separate authorization
Include psychotherapy notes, because a treating clinician may receive every note in the chart
Copy the patient's employer so hiring staff can confirm the cardiac findings

explanation: HIPAA permits disclosure of protected health information for treatment, payment, and health care operations without a separate authorization. Visit notes a treating cardiologist needs are a treatment disclosure. That permission does not cover marketing, an employer hiring decision, or psychotherapy notes, which need their own authorization.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a treatment disclosure with a release that needs a written authorization; treatment of the same patient does not wait on that form.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses ordinary visit notes with psychotherapy notes, which stay out of routine treatment disclosures and need a specific authorization.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses treatment, payment, and operations with an employer hiring inquiry, which is not a permitted disclosure on that basis.

prompt: Before any copies leave, the CMAA reviews a release that names the recipient and the records but leaves the expiration and the signature date blank.

options.text: Accept it and let staff add the recipient, purpose, and expiration after the signature
Accept it if the requesting clinic signs and a phone consent is noted in the chart
Return it until who, what, recipient, purpose, expiration, and a dated signature are set
Accept it with the patient name, the record type, and a signature, and skip the expiration

explanation: A HIPAA authorization is valid only when its core elements are complete at signing: what information, who may disclose it, who may receive it, the purpose, an expiration date or event, and the patient's signature and date. A form missing the expiration or the signature date is defective and goes back to be completed before any copies are released.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a finished authorization with a form staff may finish later; recipient, purpose, and expiration must already be present when the patient signs.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a patient authorization with the requester's signature plus verbal consent; the patient or personal representative must sign.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a partial signature block with a valid authorization; an expiration date or event is a required core element.

prompt: Yesterday's signed EHR entry lists the wrong pharmacy, and the CMAA must correct that clerical mistake under the practice's electronic documentation policy.

options.text: Overwrite the pharmacy field once a provider agrees the screen should look clean
Delete the wrong pharmacy and retype the correction under yesterday's original time
Edit the clinician's signed note directly because the mistake is clerical
Add an addendum that leaves the original pharmacy entry readable

explanation: An electronic correction is an addendum that leaves the original entry readable. The date, time, and author of the change belong in the audit trail. Overwriting, deleting, or backdating the old pharmacy hides what the record said and breaks that trail, even when the mistake was clerical.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a clean screen with a proper correction; overwriting erases the original entry instead of preserving it in an addendum.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a backdated re-entry with a correction; deleting the error and reusing yesterday's time hides when the change was actually made.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses clerical cleanup with authority to alter another clinician's signed note; the original author corrects it, or policy specifies who may addend.

prompt: A portal message asks for last year's imaging report, the request is complete, and the CMAA must choose a turnaround the privacy rule will support.

options.text: Log the request and meet the federal access deadline and any shorter state deadline
Set the due date at 90 days on the theory that HIPAA states no access deadline at all
Send the report within the hour, before anyone confirms who is asking
Let the requester pick the due date, including a demand for release tonight

explanation: HIPAA requires the practice to act on an access request within 30 calendar days, with one written 30-day extension when the rule allows it. A state deadline can be shorter. The CMAA logs the request, confirms identity before release, and does not let the requester invent a different legal clock.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the access clock with an open-ended wait; HIPAA sets a 30-day deadline with one extension, not a 90-day default.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses speed with a finished release; identity and authority come before copies go out, and same-hour release is not the legal test.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the requester's preference with the legal timeline; federal and state rules, not the caller, set the turnaround.

prompt: At a first visit, the patient asks why the receptionist is offering a Notice of Privacy Practices and requesting a signature before the exam.

options.text: It is the contract that tells a billing vendor how to store the practice's data
It tells the patient how health information may be used and what rights apply
It is handed out when someone asks for a chart copy, and at no earlier visit
It is sent to the health plan before the practice may file the first claim

explanation: The Notice of Privacy Practices tells patients how the practice may use and disclose protected health information and what rights they have. It is offered at the first service, with a good-faith effort to obtain a written acknowledgment. A refused signature is documented; the notice is still the patient's, not the vendor's or the payer's.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the patient notice with a business associate agreement; vendors are bound by that contract, not by the Notice of Privacy Practices.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the first-visit notice with a records request; the notice is offered at the first service, not saved until someone asks for copies.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the patient notice with a payer filing requirement; health plans do not receive the Notice of Privacy Practices before a claim.

prompt: The scheduler wants the full hospital history opened so a reminder call can mention the diagnosis, but the call needs the appointment time.

options.text: Open the full history, treating a reminder call as treatment so the limit would not apply
Drop required registration fields, such as date of birth, to make the chart smaller
Limit the scheduler to the least information that reminder call needs
Open every section because the scheduler signed a confidentiality pledge

explanation: The minimum-necessary standard limits use and disclosure of protected health information to what the purpose requires. A reminder needs the appointment details, not the hospital history. The treatment exception, which lets a clinician receive what care requires, does not turn a scheduling call into a reason to open the whole chart.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a scheduling reminder with a disclosure to a provider for treatment; the treatment exception does not waive the limit for a reminder call.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses minimum necessary with cutting required registration data; the standard limits use and disclosure, not collection of the legal name, date of birth, or coverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a signed pledge with permission to browse; the pledge does not expand a scheduler's access beyond the job need.

prompt: The office manager wants adult charts destroyed on one nationwide anniversary and asks which rules actually control how long those charts are kept.

options.text: HIPAA, which sets destruction of every medical record at six years after the last visit
CMS, which sets one seven-year retention period for every adult chart in the country
The minor-record formula that runs from the age of majority plus extra years
State law, together with payer and accreditation rules, for adult chart retention

explanation: How long adult medical records are kept is set by state law and by payer and accreditation requirements, and the practice follows the strictest rule that applies. HIPAA's six-year period covers privacy-program documentation such as policies and authorizations, not the clinical chart. There is no single national destruction date.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses HIPAA's six-year retention of privacy documentation with medical-record retention, which state law and payer rules govern.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a familiar seven-year figure with a national CMS mandate; no single federal period sets adult chart destruction for every practice.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses adult retention with the minor-record rule that extends keeping a chart past the age of majority.

prompt: An adult patient's spouse, listed as the emergency contact and the person who pays the copay, wants to sign a records release, and no legal document is on file.

options.text: Require a health care power of attorney or other legal authority first
Let the spouse sign, because marriage supplies personal-representative authority
Accept the signature because the emergency-contact line creates that authority
Accept the signature because paying the copay makes the spouse the representative

explanation: Under HIPAA, a personal representative is someone state law authorizes to make health care decisions for the patient, such as a health care power of attorney or a court-appointed guardian. Marriage, an emergency-contact listing, and paying the bill do not by themselves create that authority, so the CMAA verifies the document before accepting the spouse's signature.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses marriage with personal-representative status; a spouse does not automatically hold authority to sign a release for an adult patient.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an emergency-contact listing with legal authority to act for the patient or to sign a release.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses financial responsibility for a copay with authority to receive protected health information or sign an authorization.

prompt: The CMAA is ready to fax a consult note to a number recited by phone, from a machine in the open hallway, with a blank cover page.

options.text: Add any cover sheet and fax the entire chart so the recipient has full context
Verify the number, use a cover sheet, and fax from a nonpublic area
Fax it to the main office line now and call afterward to ask whether it arrived
Print the diagnosis on the cover sheet so hallway staff can route the pages

explanation: A fax of protected health information goes to a verified or preprogrammed number, with a cover sheet that carries a confidentiality notice rather than clinical details, from a machine in a nonpublic area. Checking after the fact does not undo a misdirected fax, and the full chart is more than this consult requires.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a cover sheet with a complete safeguard; faxing the entire chart exceeds what the consult needs, and the number is still unverified.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a callback after transmission with prevention; a shared main number must be confirmed before protected health information is sent.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses routing convenience with a safe cover sheet; the diagnosis is protected health information and does not belong on a page people in the hallway can read.

prompt: A coworker leaves a labeled paper face sheet on the counter and claims privacy duties attach to the electronic chart alone, so the paper copy can sit in the open.

options.text: Agree, because privacy duties attach to the electronic health record and not to paper
Treat the face sheet as protected health information because it is identifiable health information on paper
Treat the face sheet as de-identified even though the name and date of birth are still printed
File the face sheet with hiring paperwork, because employer files and the medical chart are the same category

explanation: Protected health information is individually identifiable health information in any form: paper, oral, or electronic. A labeled face sheet is protected even though it is not in the EHR. That sheet leaves the definition once it is actually de-identified. Employment files a practice holds as an employer are a separate exclusion, and that exclusion does not cover this face sheet or let it sit in the open.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the Security Rule's electronic subset with the Privacy Rule; paper and spoken identifiable health information are protected too.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a labeled face sheet with de-identified data; Safe Harbor removal of identifiers has not happened while the name and date of birth remain.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the medical chart with employment records a covered entity holds as an employer, which are excluded, and does not make this face sheet unprotected.

prompt: A life insurer emails letterhead asking for the full chart and a diagnosis summary, and the patient has signed nothing for that company.

options.text: Send the chart because the company stated a purpose on its own letterhead
Wait for a valid patient authorization or another permitted disclosure
Release the summary after writing the patient's verbal permission in the chart
Send it under the general consent to treat signed at the first visit

explanation: A life-insurance request is not treatment, payment, or health care operations. Payment means paying for health care, not underwriting a life policy. Without a valid patient authorization, or a different HIPAA permission that truly fits, the CMAA does not release the chart. Letterhead, a charted verbal okay, and consent to treat do not fill that gap.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the requester's letterhead with the patient's authorization; the company's own letter does not authorize a non-treatment disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a charted verbal okay with a HIPAA authorization, which must be written and signed and must contain the core elements.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses consent to treatment with an authorization; the first-visit consent does not name this insurer or this disclosure.

prompt: Ink is already dry on a paper progress note where the CMAA wrote the wrong date, and that page has to remain in the chart.

options.text: Erase the wrong date until the first marks can no longer be read
Draw one line through the date, initial and date the line, then write the correction
Cover the wrong date with correction fluid so the page looks untouched
Remove that page from the chart and substitute a clean sheet that hides the mistaken date

explanation: A paper correction stays legible. One line through the error, the writer's initials and the date of the correction, and the corrected entry leave both the mistake and the fix visible. Erasing, correction fluid, and pulling the page are obliteration, and the chart then cannot show what was written first.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a clean page with a proper correction; erasing until the original date is unreadable obliterates the entry.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses cosmetic cleanup with a correction; correction fluid hides the original date and is obliteration.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses replacing the page with correcting it; removing the sheet destroys the original entry instead of lining it out.

prompt: A provider says charts may be kept for whatever period the provider prefers, while the survey binder and the state statute list different schedules.

options.text: Apply the HIPAA six-year documentation rule to every clinical chart
Follow state law, payer rules, and facility policy, whichever is strictest
Follow the accreditation manual and set aside the state statute where they differ
Follow the provider's preference as long as the storage room locks

explanation: Medical-record retention has to satisfy state law, payer requirements, and the facility's own policy at the same time, so the practice keeps charts long enough to meet the strictest of those rules. An accreditation manual can add a requirement, but it does not cancel a state statute, and a provider's personal preference does not set the period.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses HIPAA's six-year retention of privacy-program documents with the retention period for the clinical chart.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses accreditation guidance with a statute; a survey standard may add a duty, but it does not override state law.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses secure storage with a legal retention period; locking the room does not let a provider choose how long charts are kept.

prompt: Front-desk credentials can open every full chart, and a coworker argues that the signed confidentiality pledge is what makes that access acceptable.

options.text: Keep full-chart access for every user who has signed the confidentiality pledge
Limit each login to the health information that person's job function needs
Treat the pledge as the switch that opens the patient's own portal
Let clinicians edit any note while front-desk staff view every chart in the system

explanation: Role-based access is how the EHR enforces the minimum-necessary standard for the workforce. Each login should reach the information that job needs, such as scheduling and demographics at the front desk, and no more. A signed pledge does not replace those limits, and it is not the patient's portal access.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a confidentiality pledge with access rights; signing the pledge does not entitle every user to every chart.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses workforce access controls with the patient portal; the portal is how the patient sees their own record, not how staff logins are scoped.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses broad clinical editing and front-desk browsing with role-based access; viewing and editing are both limited by job function.

prompt: An insulin order reads 10 U at bedtime, and the CMAA stops while entering it because that unit abbreviation is on the unsafe list.

options.text: Ask the prescriber to rewrite the dose with the word unit before it is entered
Enter 10 units, treating the letter U as an approved short form for unit
Enter 10 cc, because a handwritten U is often taken as the symbol for cubic centimeters
Replace U with IU so the insulin dose uses an international-unit abbreviation instead

explanation: The Joint Commission Do Not Use list bans U and u for unit, because the letter is mistaken for a zero, the number 4, or cc. The safe chart entry spells the word unit. The CMAA does not guess which misreading was intended and does not swap in IU, which is banned on its own.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a banned abbreviation with an approved short form; U is on the Do Not Use list and is written as the word unit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the reason U is dangerous with permission to enter cc; that misreading is why the prescriber must rewrite the dose.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses one banned abbreviation with a fix; IU is also on the Do Not Use list and is written as international unit.

prompt: Three vitamin D orders sit on the desk, and the CMAA must choose the wording that avoids the banned abbreviation IU before filing.

options.text: File 1000 international units, with those words written out
File 1000 IU, the letter form printed on most vitamin labels
File 1000 IV, reading the abbreviation as an intravenous route
File 10000, because the letters IU can be misread as the number 10 and that misreading should be stored as the dose

explanation: IU is on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list because it is mistaken for IV or for the number 10. The acceptable medication wording is the words international unit. Filing the letter form, converting it to an intravenous route, or storing the misread number 10 keeps the dangerous abbreviation in play.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a label convention with an approved chart abbreviation; IU remains on the Do Not Use list and is written out.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses IU with IV, which is the misreading the list is meant to prevent, and turns a vitamin dose into a route.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the hazard, IU looking like the number 10, with the dose that should be filed; the words international unit are what get stored.

prompt: Metformin is written 500 mg QD on the home medication list, and the patient asks the CMAA to file that line in the chart.

options.text: Ask the prescriber to replace QD with the word daily before the line is filed
Tell the patient QD means four times a day, then file the abbreviation as written
Change QD to QOD and file the metformin as an every-other-day dose
File the letters QD unchanged, because a short daily form is clearer than the full word

explanation: QD is on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list for daily, because it is mistaken for QOD, and the period after the Q can be mistaken for the letter I. The chart should say daily, written by the prescriber. The CMAA does not translate QD as four times a day, which is QID, and does not substitute the equally banned QOD.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses QD (daily) with QID (four times a day) and would file a banned abbreviation with the wrong schedule.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a fix with a swap of banned abbreviations; QOD means every other day and is on the same Do Not Use list.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses brevity with safety; QD is banned on medication documentation, and the word daily is the required form.

prompt: The patient is surprised the hospital already has yesterday's clinic note and asks which system is meant to share the record across separate organizations.

options.text: The electronic health record, built to share information across organizations
The electronic medical record, defined as the chart that travels from hospital to hospital
The practice billing ledger, which outside hospitals use as the shared clinical history
A photo of the note on a personal phone, treated as the shared legal chart once it is texted

explanation: An electronic medical record is the digital chart inside one practice. An electronic health record is built to exchange clinical information with other organizations, which is why a hospital can already hold yesterday's clinic note. The billing ledger and a personal photo are not that shared record.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the electronic medical record with the electronic health record; the in-office chart is not the system designed to move between organizations.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the billing ledger with the clinical record that health information exchange shares.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a texted photo with the legal shared record; a personal phone is not the electronic health record.

prompt: Warfarin is written QOD on a discharge medication list, and the CMAA must decide what schedule is safe to store in the chart.

options.text: Store the letters QOD, treating that short form as an approved every-other-day abbreviation
Change QOD to QD and store the warfarin as a daily dose
Ask the prescriber to replace QOD with the words every other day before filing
Read QOD as four times a day and store that dosing schedule

explanation: QOD is on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list because it is mistaken for QD (daily) or for QID (four times a day). On a medication list the safe wording is every other day, written out by the prescriber. Storing QOD, silently converting it to daily, or calling it four times a day can change a warfarin schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses QOD with an approved abbreviation; every other day must be written in words on medication documentation.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses QOD with QD; that swap turns every other day into daily and is the error the list exists to stop.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses QOD with QID, which means four times a day, and would file a schedule the order did not state.

prompt: A tablet order is written 2.0 mg, and the CMAA notices the zero after the decimal just before typing the dose into the record.

options.text: Type 2.0 mg so the electronic line copies the paper order character for character
Drop the decimal and type 20 mg as the dose the trailing zero was meant to show
Ask the prescriber to rewrite the medication dose as 2 mg with no trailing zero
Accept 2.0 mg under the precision exception that laboratories use for reported results

explanation: On medication orders and other medication documentation, a trailing zero is on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list because the decimal can be missed and 2.0 read as 20. The dose is rewritten as 2 mg. A missing leading zero, such as .5 mg written instead of 0.5 mg, is the paired problem. The precision exception is for values such as lab results, not for a tablet dose.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a literal transcription with a safe dose designation; copying 2.0 mg keeps a banned trailing zero on a medication order.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the hazard, a missed decimal turning 2.0 into 20, with the dose that should be entered.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the laboratory precision exception with a medication order; a trailing zero is not used to write a tablet strength.

prompt: A preoperative order reads MgSO4 2 g IV, and the CMAA cannot tell whether the writer meant magnesium sulfate or a morphine product.

options.text: Enter morphine sulfate, treating MS, MSO4, and MgSO4 as morphine by default
Enter magnesium sulfate now, because the letters Mg look clear enough to act on without a callback
Hold the order until the prescriber writes magnesium sulfate or morphine sulfate in full
Substitute MSO4, the short form that can stand in for either drug name

explanation: MS, MSO4, and MgSO4 are on the Joint Commission Do Not Use list because morphine sulfate and magnesium sulfate are confused with each other. The order is held until the prescriber writes the full drug name. Choosing morphine by habit, entering magnesium because the letters look familiar, or swapping in MSO4 all leave the mix-up in the chart.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the whole banned family with a default of morphine; MS can mean either drug, so guessing morphine is the error the list targets.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a familiar chemical abbreviation with a safe order; MgSO4 must be written as magnesium sulfate, not interpreted at the desk.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a substitute abbreviation with a clarification; MSO4 is itself on the Do Not Use list and does not name one drug.

prompt: The outside billing service wants the lifetime chart exported so one copay can be posted, though the charge line needs the visit date and the fee.

options.text: Export the lifetime chart, treating payment work as exempt from the minimum-necessary limit
Include the psychotherapy notes, because a billing request may gather every counseling entry
Send the visit date and the charge the billing service needs to post that copay
Refuse the billing service unless the patient signs an authorization for a marketing use

explanation: Minimum necessary applies to uses and disclosures for payment. Posting one copay needs the visit date and the charge, not the lifetime chart and not psychotherapy notes. Payment to a billing service under its agreement is not a marketing use, so a marketing authorization is the wrong gate, and the treatment exception does not apply to this payment task.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses payment with the treatment exception; minimum necessary still limits what a billing service receives for a copay.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a routine billing disclosure with access to psychotherapy notes, which are not released for ordinary payment.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses payment operations with marketing; sharing the minimum charge data with the billing service does not require a marketing authorization.

prompt: Between appointments, a coworker opens a neighbor's laboratory result on the scheduling computer with no work task connected to that neighbor.

options.text: Allow the lookup, because a staff sign-on may open any chart during the workday
Allow the lookup if the coworker adds a note that the reason was personal curiosity
Stop the lookup, because curiosity is not a job need for those results
Allow the lookup, because the neighbor once signed a general consent to be treated

explanation: Workforce use of protected health information is limited to the job purpose. Opening a neighbor's lab result out of curiosity fails the minimum-necessary standard even if the scheduling login can technically reach the screen. A late note about curiosity, a workday sign-on, and consent to treat do not create a job need.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses having a login with permission to open any chart; access is limited to the information the job requires.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses documenting a personal reason with authorizing it; writing that the lookup was curiosity does not make the use permitted.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses consent to treatment with staff permission to browse a neighbor's results for a nonwork reason.

prompt: After showing a photo identification, a patient asks for a copy of her after-visit summary and recent lab results to take home, and no outside party is named.

options.text: Refuse until a third-party authorization form names an outside recipient
Hand the copies to her spouse at the window so the pickup is quicker
Give her the copy as an access request once her identity is confirmed
Wait for her health plan to approve the request before any pages are copied

explanation: A patient has a right of access to her own designated record set, including the after-visit summary and lab results. That request is not a third-party authorization, and it does not need the health plan's approval. The CMAA confirms identity and gives the copy to the patient. Handing it to a spouse is a different disclosure.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the patient's right of access with an authorization used to disclose records to someone else.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a faster family pickup with the patient's own access; the spouse is not the requester and has no authority on these facts.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a payer utilization step with the right of access; the health plan does not have to approve the patient's copy of her own record.

prompt: During a busy check-in, a medical assistant offers a shared EHR password so two people can document under a single sign-on.

options.text: Share the password and put both sets of initials in a free-text comment
Use the provider login, because the audit trail stores the patient name rather than the user
Post the password on the monitor so the next shift can keep the same session open
Have each person sign in under a personal account so the audit trail shows who acted

explanation: The EHR audit trail is useful only when each workforce member uses a unique sign-on. A shared password, the provider's login, or a password on the monitor makes it impossible to see who viewed or changed the chart. Initials in a comment do not repair an audit record that names the wrong user.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a free-text initial with an audit control; a shared password still records one user for two people's work.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the patient identifier with the user identifier; the audit trail is supposed to show which workforce member acted.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses shift convenience with access control; a posted password lets anyone continue a session under someone else's name.

prompt: An attorney presents a subpoena at the window and wants to carry the patient's chart copies out within the next few minutes.

options.text: Hand over the chart immediately, because a subpoena replaces any review of the request
Refuse the request, treating a court process as unable to reach the medical chart
Release the chart if the attorney shows a business card and promises an authorization later
Hold the copies and follow the legal-request process with the privacy lead

explanation: A subpoena is not a signal to hand the chart across the counter. HIPAA permits disclosure of what a court order expressly authorizes, and a subpoena without a court order needs the required patient notice or protective-order assurances. The CMAA holds the copies and follows the practice's legal-request steps with the privacy lead.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses any subpoena with an immediate release; a subpoena still has to meet the privacy-rule conditions before copies leave.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses caution with a total ban; a proper court order can require disclosure of the information it names.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses professional courtesy with authority; a business card and a promise of a later authorization do not permit release.

prompt: A patient viewing the portal says the allergy list is wrong and asks the CMAA to erase that line from the signed electronic note today.

options.text: Delete the allergy on the spot so the portal matches what the patient remembers
Overwrite the signed note and drop the original line from the audit history
Turn the patient away, because a signed electronic note is closed to patient questions
Accept a written amendment request and route it to the author for review under policy

explanation: HIPAA gives the patient a right to request an amendment of protected health information in the designated record set. The CMAA accepts the written request and routes it to the author. The original allergy line stays in the record, and the audit trail stays intact, whether the request is granted or denied. A granted amendment is appended or linked to that line and does not erase it. The front desk does not delete a signed entry.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a patient request with authority to delete; the front desk does not erase a signed allergy line on the patient's word.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an amendment with obliteration; overwriting and stripping the audit history destroy the original entry.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a signed note with a record the patient cannot challenge; the patient may request an amendment, and the author reviews it.

prompt: A patient phones to cancel the authorization that allowed records to go to a life insurer, after several pages were already faxed yesterday under that form.

options.text: Keep sending, because a phone call cannot affect an authorization that has already been used
Demand that the insurer return yesterday's pages and tell the patient the disclosure has been erased
Keep sending updates until the printed expiration, because a revocation cannot take effect any sooner
Get a written revocation, stop later releases, and leave yesterday's fax as already made

explanation: A HIPAA authorization may be revoked in writing, except to the extent the practice has already relied on it. The CMAA asks for a written revocation, makes no further disclosures under that form, and documents the request. Yesterday's fax was already made and is not pulled back or described to the patient as erased.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the need for a written revocation with permission to keep disclosing; the next step is to obtain the writing and stop further releases.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses revocation with a rewind; a revocation does not undo a disclosure the practice already made in reliance on the authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the expiration date with the revocation rule; a valid written revocation stops later disclosures before the printed expiration.

prompt: The EHR is down, the CMAA captured the visit on the approved downtime form, and the provider asks where that paper belongs once the system returns.

options.text: Discard the paper once the EHR is back, because downtime notes are scratch work
Leave the form in a desk drawer and leave that visit blank in the EHR
Email a photo of the form to a personal inbox so the official chart can stay empty of the outage
Enter the downtime form into the EHR and keep it in the legal record per policy

explanation: Downtime documentation is part of the visit, not scratch paper. When the EHR returns, the approved form is entered or scanned into the chart and retained with the legal health record under the outage policy. Discarding it, hiding it in a drawer, or emailing it to a personal inbox leaves the official record incomplete and puts patient information outside the chart.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a downtime form with disposable scratch paper; the visit was documented on that form and belongs in the legal record.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses private storage with filing; a drawer copy and a blank electronic visit omit the encounter from the designated record.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a personal inbox with the chart; emailing the form outside the record both loses the entry and exposes the information.

prompt: During charge capture, a coworker asks the CMAA what the procedure code set on the encounter form is meant to describe.

options.text: Procedures and services the provider performed
Diagnoses and the reasons for the patient's visit
Supplies, drugs, and ambulance services on the claim
Inpatient facility procedures performed in the hospital

explanation: CPT, also called HCPCS Level I, reports procedures and services. The CMAA can recognize that category on a charge ticket, but choosing the specific code belongs to the coder, not the assistant.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses CPT with ICD-10-CM, which reports diagnoses and the reason for the visit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses CPT with HCPCS Level II, which reports supplies, drugs, and ambulance services.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses CPT with ICD-10-PCS, which reports inpatient facility procedures.

prompt: A payer returns a claim with a timely filing denial after the office sent it past the plan's submission deadline.

options.text: The visit was done without the payer's advance approval
The claim arrived after the payer's filing deadline
The payer missed its own window for finishing the claim
Coverage had not been checked before the claim was sent

explanation: A timely filing denial means the claim reached the payer after that plan's submission deadline. The office tracks each payer's limit and corrects or appeals inside that payer's rules. It is separate from an authorization or eligibility denial.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a timely filing denial with a missing prior-authorization denial.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the provider's late submission with a payer processing delay under prompt-pay rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a timely filing denial with an eligibility denial from unverified coverage.

prompt: A patient hands the CMAA cards for an employer plan and a spouse plan. What must the assistant determine before either policy is billed?

options.text: How much the patient owes once the deductible is met
Whether this visit needs approval before it is performed
Which plan pays first when the patient has two coverages
Which clinician is paid when two doctors bill one service

explanation: Coordination of benefits sets which plan pays first when a patient has more than one policy, so the secondary plan is not billed as if it were primary. It does not calculate the cost share on a single plan, and it is not a referral rule or a duplicate-claim edit.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses coordination of benefits with cost sharing owed under a single plan after the deductible.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coordination of benefits with preauthorization required by one plan's utilization rules.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses two plans for one patient with two clinicians billing the same service, which is a duplicate-claim edit.

prompt: Before a Medicare patient receives a service the plan may not cover, the CMAA must identify the form that warns of possible financial liability.

options.text: A state Medicaid request for approval before the service
A commercial plan's payment summary mailed after the claim
Medicare's later notice of how a processed claim was paid
A Medicare notice that the service may not be covered

explanation: An Advance Beneficiary Notice is given to an Original Medicare patient before a service Medicare may not cover, so the patient knows they may have to pay. It is issued before the service, not after the claim is processed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the Medicare Advance Beneficiary Notice with a state Medicaid prior-authorization request.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the Advance Beneficiary Notice with a commercial explanation of benefits sent after payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the Advance Beneficiary Notice with the Medicare Summary Notice, which is sent after the claim is processed.

prompt: While preparing a chart for the coder, the CMAA is asked what should determine the diagnosis code and its level of specificity.

options.text: The provider's note, at the specificity that note supports
