The referral diagnosis, even when the visit note differs
The preprinted code closest to the patient's complaint
A probable or rule-out diagnosis from the outpatient visit

explanation: Diagnosis codes follow the provider's documentation, taken to the highest specificity that note supports. The CMAA does not assign the code. On outpatient claims, probable or rule-out wording is not coded; the coder uses what the provider actually documented.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the referral line with the encounter documentation, which governs the diagnosis when the two differ.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a nearby preprinted superbill code with a code supported at the specificity in the note.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses inpatient uncertain-diagnosis habits with outpatient rules, which do not code probable or rule-out diagnoses.

prompt: The billing lead asks the CMAA which submitted claim is clean enough for the payer to process without stopping for missing data.

options.text: One the primary payer has already paid in full
One with complete, accurate data the payer can process
One sent electronically rather than on a paper CMS-1500
One that passed the scrubber even if the payer later pends it

explanation: A clean claim has complete, accurate data so the payer can process it without stopping for a defect such as a missing subscriber identifier, date of birth, or place of service. Being paid, being electronic, or passing a scrubber while the payer still pends it are different outcomes.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a clean claim with a paid claim; a clean claim can still leave a patient balance.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses clean-claim content with the submission format; a paper claim can be clean and an electronic claim can be incomplete.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses clearinghouse edits with payer acceptance; a claim the payer pends for missing data is not clean.

prompt: At the end of clinic, the manager asks what the day sheet and the accounts receivable ledger are meant to follow.

options.text: That day's appointments, no-shows, and cancellations
Payroll hours, overtime, and staff reimbursements
Charges, payments, adjustments, and balances still open
Supply orders, vendor invoices, and payments the office owes

explanation: The day sheet and accounts receivable ledger follow charges, payments, adjustments, and balances still owed to the practice by patients and payers. Accurate posting is what lets the office explain a bill later.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the day sheet with the schedule, which tracks appointments, no-shows, and cancellations.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses patient accounts receivable with payroll and staff reimbursements.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses accounts receivable, money owed to the office, with accounts payable owed to vendors.

prompt: A coder reviewing today's charges asks the CMAA which same-day pattern modifier 25 is used to flag.

options.text: A bilateral procedure done in the same operative session
A distinct procedure performed at a separate site that day
A clinical lab test repeated the same day for a new result
A significant, separate evaluation on the day of a procedure

explanation: Modifier 25 flags a significant, separately identifiable evaluation on the same day as a procedure, and the note must show that visit is distinct from the procedure's usual work. The coder applies the modifier; the CMAA recognizes the pattern and routes the note rather than coding the claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses modifier 25 with modifier 50, which reports a bilateral procedure in one session.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses modifier 25 with modifier 59, which reports a distinct procedure at a separate site.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses modifier 25 with modifier 91, which reports a repeat clinical lab test on the same day.

prompt: A patient calls confused about a bill, so the CMAA reviews what a mailed statement should show before sending a replacement.

options.text: Dates of service, charges, payments, and the amount due
The balance due alone, so line items do not add confusion
Charges and the balance, leaving payments to the payer notice
The specialty printed on the envelope, such as oncology billing

explanation: A patient statement should show dates of service, charges, payments, adjustments, and the amount due, with a contact for billing questions. The patient needs those lines to see how the balance was reached. The envelope should use a neutral return address.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a clear itemized statement with a balance-only bill, which hides the dates and payments the patient needs.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the statement with the payer's explanation of benefits; insurance payments belong on the statement too.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a useful statement with a specialty printed on the envelope, which can expose health information in the mail.

prompt: A patient asks whether preauthorization and precertification are the same kind of step, and the CMAA explains what both require.

options.text: A guarantee the payer will pay once the service is approved
Payer approval required before certain services for coverage
The patient's signed consent to the procedure and its risks
A medical-necessity review that starts after the claim is sent

explanation: Preauthorization and precertification are payer approval steps required before certain services if the plan is to consider coverage. Neither step promises payment, because eligibility, benefits, and medical necessity can still lead to a denial.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses prior approval with a guarantee of payment, which the approval does not provide.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses payer authorization with informed consent between the patient and the provider.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses approval before the service with retrospective review after the claim is submitted.

prompt: A new patient asks why early visits this year are billed to them even though the card shows the plan is active.

options.text: A fixed amount collected at every covered office visit
The amount paid before the plan starts paying covered services
The percentage of allowed cost paid after that amount is met
The monthly sum paid to keep the insurance plan in force

explanation: The deductible is what the patient pays toward covered services before the plan begins to pay. An active card means the policy is in force; it does not mean the deductible has been met. Copay, coinsurance, and premium are different patient costs.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the deductible with a copay, the fixed amount due at a visit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the deductible with coinsurance, the percentage paid after the deductible is met.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the deductible with the premium, the amount paid to keep the plan active.

prompt: The office must bill a physician outpatient visit, and the CMAA has to choose the claim form used for professional services.

options.text: The UB-04 institutional claim used by hospital facilities
The CMS-1500 claim form used for professional billing
The payment summary a payer sends after it processes a claim
The itemized statement mailed to the patient after posting

explanation: Professional services by a physician are billed on the CMS-1500 or its electronic equivalent. The UB-04 is the institutional claim used by facilities. A payment summary and a patient statement come after the claim is processed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the CMS-1500 professional claim with the UB-04 used for hospital facility billing.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the claim form with a payer's explanation of benefits or Medicare Summary Notice.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the claim form with the patient statement produced after payments are posted.

prompt: While checking insurance, the assistant discovers two current health plans on file and needs to know when benefit coordination is required.

options.text: One plan demands a primary-care referral before a specialist
More than one plan may cover the same services for this patient
A single claim is split between the deductible and coinsurance
The old plan has ended and the new plan has no overlap

explanation: Coordination of benefits is required when more than one plan may pay for the same services, so the office can bill in primary-then-secondary order. A referral rule, cost sharing inside one plan, and a plan change with no overlap do not create that step.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses coordination of benefits with a gatekeeper referral required by a single plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coordination of benefits with deductible and coinsurance sharing inside one plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses overlapping coverage with a clean plan change, which is billed only to the plan in effect.

prompt: After the visit, the provider marks the encounter form, and a trainee asks the CMAA what that superbill is supposed to list.

options.text: Payments and adjustments posted to accounts that day
Common diagnoses and procedures that support charge capture
Itemized charges and the balance due after insurance pays
Services already approved and their authorization numbers

explanation: The encounter form, or superbill, lists common diagnoses and procedures so the provider can mark the visit and the office can capture charges. The coder uses that marked form with the note; the form itself is not a payment log or a statement.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the superbill with the day sheet, which records payments and adjustments posted that day.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the superbill with the patient statement, which shows charges and the balance after insurance.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the superbill with the authorization log, where approval numbers are tracked.

prompt: If a claim is denied for missing information, the CMAA should generally

options.text: File a formal appeal with the payer before reviewing the denial reason code
Review the denial reason, correct the claim/documentation, and resubmit or appeal
Bill the patient for the full amount until the payer reprocesses the claim
Resubmit the same claim right away, since most missing-info denials clear

explanation: A missing-information denial means the payer stopped the claim for a defect, not that it decided coverage. The CMAA reads the reason code, adds the missing field or record, and resubmits the corrected claim, using an appeal only when the payer's notice requires that path. Repeating the same claim or billing the patient leaves the defect in place.

distractorExplanations.a: Missing-information denials are fixed by correcting and resubmitting; appealing without reading the reason code wastes time.
distractorExplanations.c: Shifting a payer-side billing error to the patient is improper; the office must correct the claim before billing any patient balance.
distractorExplanations.d: Resubmitting an unchanged claim triggers a duplicate or repeat denial; the missing information must be added first.

prompt: At check-in, eligibility shows a fixed dollar amount due for today's covered office visit, separate from the annual deductible.

options.text: A copay, the fixed amount due for this covered visit
The rest of the deductible, collected in full before the visit
Coinsurance, a percentage of the allowed charge for today
The premium, the monthly cost of keeping this plan active

explanation: A fixed amount due for a covered visit, and kept separate from the deductible, is the copay. The CMAA collects it when eligibility says it applies. Coinsurance is a percentage, and the premium is the cost of keeping the policy, not a visit charge.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a per-visit copay with the deductible, which is the amount paid before the plan starts paying.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a fixed copay with coinsurance, which is a percentage of the allowed amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the copay collected at check-in with the premium paid to keep coverage in force.

prompt: After the plan has started paying, the patient asks what name belongs to the percentage still owed on the allowed amount.

options.text: Coinsurance, the patient's percentage of the allowed amount
A second deductible that starts again at every later visit
A flat copay that replaces any percentage on the visit
The premium the insurer bills each month to keep coverage

explanation: After the deductible is met, the patient's percentage of the allowed amount is coinsurance. The CMAA names that share so the patient knows what remains their responsibility. It is not a new deductible, a copay, or the premium.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coinsurance with a deductible that resets at each visit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a percentage share with a copay, which is a fixed visit amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses coinsurance owed for a service with the premium that keeps the plan active.

prompt: The assessment on today's note is blank, and a coworker urges the CMAA to pick a likely diagnosis code so the claim can be sent.

options.text: Return the chart so the provider documents the assessment
Reuse the diagnosis from the patient's visit a year ago
Enter a frequently used diagnosis so the claim is not held
Ask the patient which diagnosis should appear on the claim

explanation: A CMAA does not assign diagnosis codes. With the assessment blank, the chart goes back to the provider, and the coder selects the code from the completed note. Guessing a code can bill a diagnosis the provider did not document.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an old encounter's diagnosis with documentation of today's assessment.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a frequently used code with a code supported by today's provider note.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the patient's preference with the provider's documented assessment.

prompt: Before the batch goes to the clearinghouse, the CMAA sees that the subscriber number on the claim differs from the insurance card.

options.text: Correct the subscriber number so it agrees with the card
Transmit the claim and expect the payer to repair the number
Drop the insurance and bill the patient the full office charge
Edit the diagnosis so the claim looks complete enough to send

explanation: A clean claim carries a subscriber number that agrees with the card and the payer's file. The CMAA corrects that field before transmission. Sending a known mismatch, billing the patient to avoid the edit, or changing the diagnosis does not make the claim clean.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses front-end correction of a bad subscriber number with hoping the payer will repair it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a data fix on a covered claim with shifting the full charge to the patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a subscriber-number error with a diagnosis change, which does not repair the identifier.

prompt: The eligibility screen shows none of the annual deductible met, the remainder exceeds today's allowed amount, and the service is subject to the deductible.

options.text: A flat copay, because the insurance coverage is already active
Nothing for the visit, because the premium is already paid
The allowed amount, applied to the deductible still unmet
A coinsurance percentage, as if the deductible were already waived

explanation: When the service applies to the deductible and the remaining deductible is larger than the allowed amount, the patient owes that allowed amount and it credits the deductible. Coinsurance waits until the deductible is met. A copay and the premium are different obligations.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses deductible responsibility with a copay just because coverage is active.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the premium, which keeps the plan in force, with the deductible still owed for this service.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an unmet deductible with coinsurance, which applies after the deductible is met.

prompt: A specialist procedure next week is listed as requiring plan approval, and the patient asks to have it placed on the schedule.

options.text: Schedule it and note that approval can be requested afterward
Accept the patient's consent form in place of plan approval
Obtain the plan's authorization before the procedure is performed
Send the claim first and ask for approval after the payer receives it

explanation: When the benefit check says a procedure requires authorization, the CMAA obtains that approval before the service and keeps the authorization number for the claim. Consent is not a substitute, and billing first risks a denial. Approval still does not guarantee the final payment.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses scheduling ahead of a required authorization with approval that can be added after the service.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the patient's informed consent with preauthorization from the payer.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses preauthorization, which happens before the service, with a request made after the claim is submitted.

prompt: Checkout staff see a set specialist amount on the card that eligibility still shows as due, while the patient expects a percentage of the charge.

options.text: Compute a percentage because every covered visit uses one
Apply the entire office charge to the deductible before any set amount
Collect the set specialist amount that eligibility shows as due
Skip that amount because a met deductible ends further sharing

explanation: The set amount eligibility still shows for this specialist visit is the copay, and the CMAA collects it. Coinsurance is a percentage and applies when the plan says so. A deductible does not cancel a copay the eligibility screen still lists as due.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a listed copay with coinsurance, the percentage of the allowed amount.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a due copay with posting the entire charge to the deductible first.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a met deductible with the end of all cost sharing, including a copay eligibility still shows.

prompt: A birth date on the claim differs from the date stored in the payer eligibility file, and the nightly batch is ready to transmit.

options.text: Transmit now and file an appeal if the payer rejects the date
Delete the birth date and let the payer insert the correct one
Correct the birth date so it agrees with the payer's file
Replace the birth date with the date of today's appointment

explanation: A birth date that differs from the payer's eligibility file keeps the claim from being clean. The CMAA corrects the claim so the birth date matches that file before the batch is sent. Appealing a known mismatch, deleting the date, or substituting the visit date does not repair the field.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses correcting a demographic error before submission with appealing a rejection afterward.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a clean claim, which includes the birth date, with leaving that field blank for the payer.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the patient's birth date with the date of service, which belongs in a different field.

prompt: An approved procedure from yesterday leads the patient to believe the insurer must pay the provider's billed charge in full.

options.text: Approval means the plan must pay the provider's full billed charge
Approval removes any need to confirm eligibility on the date of service
Approval does not promise the plan will pay the provider's billed charge
Approval means the patient will owe no copay, deductible, or coinsurance

explanation: Preauthorization means the plan gave a required approval to consider the service. It does not promise payment of the billed charge, it does not replace an eligibility check, and it does not erase copays, deductibles, or coinsurance. Payment still depends on the benefits and the claim.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses prior approval with a promise that the plan will pay the full billed charge.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses authorization with eligibility, which still has to be confirmed for the date of service.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses authorization with a waiver of copay, deductible, and coinsurance.

prompt: A coworker asks the assistant to choose a procedure code from a cheat sheet so the professional claim can leave this afternoon.

options.text: Pick the cheat-sheet line that fits a routine office visit
Copy the procedure used for a similar patient seen yesterday
Route the provider's marked encounter form to the coder
Leave the procedure blank and release the claim this afternoon

explanation: Choosing procedure codes is the coder's work. The CMAA confirms the provider marked the encounter form and routes that form to the coder. A cheat sheet, another patient's code, or a blank claim would have the assistant coding in the coder's place.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the CMAA's charge-capture role with selecting a procedure code from a cheat sheet.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses this patient's documented service with a code copied from another patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses routing a marked form to the coder with releasing a claim that has no procedure code.

prompt: Once this patient's deductible has been satisfied, the plan still uses a percentage share and the visit has no fixed amount due.

options.text: A new deductible that begins again as soon as one is met
The monthly premium added on top of the charge for this visit
No further patient share, because the deductible ends cost sharing
The coinsurance percentage of the plan's allowed amount

explanation: After the deductible is met, a plan that uses coinsurance still expects the patient's percentage of the allowed amount when the visit has no copay. Meeting the deductible does not open a new deductible, and it does not make later visits free. The premium is separate from this visit.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses coinsurance after the deductible with a deductible that starts over once it is met.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the visit's coinsurance with the premium paid to keep the plan active.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses meeting the deductible with the end of cost sharing on a plan that still has coinsurance.

prompt: The imaging study on tomorrow's schedule has no approval number, and the benefit check says the plan requires approval before the study.

options.text: Post the charge and submit the claim with no approval number
Tell the patient the study is excluded from the plan's benefits
Change the order to a different study that needs no approval
Request the plan's authorization before the study is performed

explanation: When the benefit check requires approval and no authorization number is on file, the CMAA requests authorization before the study. Submitting without it invites a denial. A missing number does not by itself mean the study is a noncovered benefit, and the assistant does not change the order.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a service that still needs preauthorization with a claim that can go out without an approval number.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a missing authorization with a benefit exclusion; the study may be covered once it is approved.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses obtaining approval for the ordered study with substituting a different service.

prompt: A blank encounter form arrives with no service marked, and a teammate suggests the CMAA fill in a procedure so billing can proceed.

options.text: Choose a procedure that matches the type of appointment booked
Reuse the procedure listed on the patient's previous encounter
Ask the patient which service should be placed on the claim
Send the form back so the provider documents the service

explanation: The CMAA does not invent a procedure for a blank encounter form. The form goes back to the provider to document the service that was performed, and the coder assigns the code. Billing from the appointment type, a prior visit, or the patient's guess can claim a service that did not happen.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the appointment type with the service the provider must document before coding.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses today's unmarked visit with the procedure on a previous encounter.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the patient's description with the provider's documentation of the service.

prompt: An in-network patient's percentage share is being explained, and the patient asks why it is not taken from the office's full fee.

options.text: The percentage should be taken from the office's full billed fee
The percentage is really a flat amount due at every visit
The percentage is the sum paid before the plan pays anything
The percentage applies to the payer's allowed amount

explanation: For an in-network claim, coinsurance is the patient's percentage of the payer's allowed amount, not of the office's full fee. A flat amount at each visit is a copay. The amount paid before the plan pays is the deductible. The CMAA explains the share from the allowed amount.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses coinsurance on the allowed amount with a percentage of the office's full billed fee.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses coinsurance with a copay, the flat amount due at a visit.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coinsurance, which follows the deductible, with the deductible itself.

prompt: A benefit check flags this service as needing plan approval first, and the patient is ready to book it today as a covered visit.

options.text: Book it as covered and let the later claim prove medical necessity
Collect toward the deductible and skip the approval call entirely
Tell the patient to phone the plan after the visit is finished
Start plan approval before booking the service as covered

explanation: A service the benefit check flags for approval is not treated as covered until preauthorization is started under the plan's rule. Booking first, skipping the call because a deductible was collected, or asking the patient to call after the visit leaves the claim exposed to a denial.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses preauthorization before the service with hoping the submitted claim will establish medical necessity.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses collecting toward the deductible with a waiver of the required approval call.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses staff obtaining preauthorization before the visit with the patient calling the plan afterward.

prompt: During check-in, a patient starts describing a new symptom while glancing at the floor and lowering their voice. What should the CMAA do first?

options.text: Paraphrase, clarify, and attend to tone and posture before moving on
Keep entering insurance data while composing a reply in your head
Finish every screen field before looking up from the monitor
Reassure them quickly that the visit will be fine so they stop describing the symptom

explanation: Active listening means hearing the words and the nonverbal cues, then paraphrasing and clarifying so the symptom is captured before registration moves on. A reply or a reassurance that cuts the story short misses details the clinician will need.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses multitasking with listening; planning a reply while typing splits attention and drops the lowered voice.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats screen completion as the first task and ignores posture and tone, which carry meaning the patient has not said plainly.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses quick reassurance with listening; cutting the story off is a barrier, not proof the concern was understood.

prompt: A patient slams a clipboard on the counter, raises their voice about a long wait, and steps closer to the CMAA. Which response fits de-escalation?

options.text: Tell the patient to leave and book another day before hearing the complaint
Stay calm, set a boundary, and involve a supervisor or security
Repeat the late-arrival policy more firmly until the patient accepts it
Handle the outburst alone so clinicians are not pulled from other patients

explanation: A hostile approach is handled with a calm tone, a clear limit, and help when safety is in question. Slamming a clipboard and stepping in close is a reason to involve a supervisor or security, then document the incident under office policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses dismissal with de-escalation; sending the patient away before hearing the complaint usually raises the conflict.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a louder policy lecture with a boundary; repeating rules at an angry patient escalates rather than settling the desk.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats staffing convenience as safety; a threatening outburst needs a supervisor or security, not a solo confrontation.

prompt: A patient says they are frightened about a biopsy and starts to cry at the front desk. Which response shows empathy rather than sympathy?

options.text: Say you feel sorry for them and that the situation is truly pitiful
Cry along with them so they see you share that same fear
Recognize the fear without taking on that same emotion
Skip past the feeling and hurry them straight into an exam room

explanation: Empathy is understanding the patient's feeling and showing that understanding while the CMAA stays professionally steady. Pity, and matching the patient's distress, are sympathy or emotional contagion, not the front-desk skill.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses sympathy with empathy; feeling sorry and calling the situation pitiful is pity, not understanding without pity.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses shared distress with empathy; taking on the same fear pulls the CMAA out of a steady professional stance.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses task speed with empathy; rushing past the tears skips the acknowledgment the patient needs at the desk.

prompt: Two coworkers in the break room ask the CMAA what procedure a well-known local coach is having this afternoon. What should the CMAA say?

options.text: Share the procedure, since everyone in the clinic works under the same roof
Describe the procedure but leave the coach's name out of the story
Give the details if the coworker says they are a close family friend
Refuse to discuss that patient's care with staff who are not involved

explanation: Confidentiality means patient information stays with people who need it for their job. Curiosity, a shared workplace, a dropped name, or a claimed friendship does not authorize a break-room disclosure about the coach's procedure.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses working in the same building with a need to know; PHI goes only to staff involved in that patient's care.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses removing a name with de-identification; a procedure plus a public role can still identify the coach.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a claimed friendship with authority to receive PHI; friendship is not a personal-representative status.

prompt: A parent offers their 10-year-old child to translate consent instructions for a grandparent who speaks little English. What should the CMAA arrange?

options.text: A qualified interpreter for the consent talk, rather than the child
Louder, slower English so the grandparent can catch the main idea
Gestures for the risky parts, with a nod counted as understanding
Skipping the consent questions until some other relative can return later

explanation: Consent instructions for a patient with limited English should go through a qualified interpreter. A minor child may omit, soften, or misunderstand the content, and the conversation can expose the child to private health details.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses hearing with language access; speaking louder does not translate risks, benefits, or alternatives.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses mime with informed consent; gestures cannot carry the content a consent conversation has to include.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats delay as a substitute for interpreting; the consent questions still have to be completed with a qualified interpreter.

prompt: A long-time patient asks the CMAA to connect on a personal social account and offers a gift card for moving their visit ahead of others. What boundary applies?

options.text: Accept the social request so the patient feels more engaged with the office
Avoid a dual relationship built on gifts and off-channel contact
Take the gift card and move that visit ahead as a one-time courtesy
Share a personal problem first so the relationship feels more mutual

explanation: Professional boundaries bar dual relationships that trade special access for gifts or private contact. Scheduling and messages stay on office channels, and the gift policy exists so one patient cannot buy a better place in line.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses engagement with a personal social tie; private accounts move communication off the practice's channels.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a courtesy with a boundary; moving a visit up for a gift card is favoritism and a conflict of interest.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses mutual self-disclosure with rapport; the visit should stay on the patient's needs, not the CMAA's personal life.

prompt: At the nurses' station the CMAA hears two coworkers naming a patient and joking about that patient's STI results. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Wait to see whether the same pair gossips about the patient again tomorrow
Call the patient immediately and suggest they file a complaint on their own
Remind them of privacy rules and report the talk if policy requires it
Leave the jokes for the privacy officer to catch on a later chart audit

explanation: Every workforce member helps protect privacy. An overheard disclosure of STI details is stopped when it happens, and the CMAA follows office policy if a supervisor or privacy officer must be told. Spoken gossip will not show up on an access log.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a single disclosure as harmless until it repeats; the patient's STI information is already being shared.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a coworker warning with breach notification; telling the patient is the privacy officer's role under policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an EHR audit with spoken gossip; access logs do not capture a joke told at the nurses' station.

prompt: A patient scheduled for a procedure asks the CMAA to explain the risks and complete the consent form before the physician arrives. How should the CMAA respond?

options.text: Explain the risks yourself, since you scheduled the procedure and hold the form
Ask the medical assistant to cover the risks while rooming the patient
Send the risk discussion to risk management to handle by phone
Let the performing provider explain the risks while you manage the form

explanation: Disclosure of risks, benefits, and alternatives for a procedure belongs to the provider who performs it. The CMAA may prepare, witness, or file the consent form, but that logistics role does not replace the clinician's conversation with the patient.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses scheduling and form handling with informed consent; a CMAA does not disclose procedural risks in the physician's place.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses rooming support with the consent duty; clinical staff may reinforce teaching, but the performing provider holds the disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses form design with the consent talk; risk management audits forms and does not replace the provider at the bedside.

prompt: A patient arrives and learns the CMAA registered them under another person's date of birth, so the visit was nearly cancelled. How should the CMAA recover the encounter?

options.text: Apologize, correct the record, and name a prevention step without blaming the patient
Offer a courtesy discount and leave the wrong date of birth on the record
Correct the date of birth quietly and hope the patient does not notice the mistake
Apologize and name the coworker who typed the wrong date of birth into the chart

explanation: Service recovery after a registration error is an apology, a real correction of the identity fields, and a concrete step so the mix-up is not repeated. Blame pointed at the patient or at a named coworker does not rebuild trust, and a discount leaves the bad data in place.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a discount with a correction; the wrong date of birth will still break later identity checks and claims.
distractorExplanations.c: Skips the acknowledgment that rebuilds trust; a silent edit hides the error the patient already experienced.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses recovery with blame; naming a coworker makes the apology about fault instead of the fix and the prevention step.

prompt: A patient repeatedly comments on a coworker's body while that coworker asks them to stop. The coworker tells the CMAA they feel unsafe filing alone. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Urge the coworker to settle it privately with the patient before any report to HR
Report the conduct under HR policy so staff have a respectful workplace
Wait until another employee witnesses the comments before anyone reports them
Treat the comments as outside policy because the speaker is a patient, not an employee

explanation: Harassment of staff is reported through the practice HR policy, including when the person responsible is a patient. A second witness is not required to start that report, and people who report should be protected from retaliation rather than pushed into a private settlement.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses informal peacemaking with the reporting path; requiring a private settlement first can silence the coworker.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses evidence rules with the duty to report; the coworker's account is enough to start the HR process.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the harasser's role with the practice's duty; patient status does not place harassment of staff outside the policy.

prompt: The CMAA must leave a voicemail asking a patient to call back about a lab result. No one answers, and the greeting is a shared family mailbox. What belongs in the message?

options.text: The test name and the result, because the greeting uses the patient's own voice
Only the minimum the policy allows, such as the practice name and a callback number
The result, left so a spouse who hears it can pass the news along
The result, once whoever calls back recites the patient's date of birth

explanation: A shared family mailbox can be heard by people other than the patient. The message should carry only what office policy treats as the minimum necessary, typically who is calling and a callback number, not the test name or the result.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the patient's voice on a greeting with a private line; other household members can still play the message.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a spouse who shares a phone with someone authorized to receive results; marriage alone is not that permission.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses knowing a birth date with identity and authority; a third party who recites it is still not cleared for the result.

prompt: A patient insists the front desk promised a same-day visit and becomes tearful when told the schedule is full. The promise is not in the record. Which reply is empathetic and still professional?

options.text: Agree that a same-day visit was promised so the patient will calm down
Acknowledge the frustration, stay professional, and offer the next opening
Describe your own missed appointment so the patient feels less alone
Book the visit today despite a full schedule because the patient is upset

explanation: Empathy names the frustration and keeps the conversation useful without agreeing to a promise the record does not show. It does not require a personal story from the CMAA or setting the schedule rules aside for one tearful encounter.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses soothing with honesty; agreeing to a same-day promise that is not in the record states a fact the desk cannot support.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses personal disclosure with empathy; the CMAA's own missed visit moves the focus off the opening that can be offered.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses kindness with opening a full schedule; empathy names the frustration while the next real opening is what the desk can offer.

prompt: An imaging-center representative tells the CMAA they will pay a personal bonus for every patient the desk sends to that center. Which description fits this offer?

options.text: An ordinary referral, because the center is one the provider already uses
A kickback that creates a referral conflict and should be refused
Harmless, as long as the CMAA also declines holiday gifts from patients
Acceptable, because relatives would still be booked under the same rules

explanation: A personal payment for steering patients to one vendor is a kickback. It puts the CMAA's gain ahead of the patient's interest, which is an ethical conflict and can violate anti-kickback rules. The offer is refused and reported on the compliance path.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a provider-selected site with a paid steer; a personal bonus to the CMAA is not ordinary referral workflow.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses gift-policy compliance with this deal; declining a patient gift does not make a referral bonus acceptable.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses fair booking of relatives with referral ethics; equal rules for family do not clean up a payment for where patients are sent.

prompt: An adult patient with limited English asks for help understanding postoperative instructions. A daughter volunteers, and a billing coworker says they studied the language in school. What should the CMAA use?

options.text: The daughter, because an adult relative can relay clinical instructions
A qualified interpreter service, as facility policy directs
The billing coworker, who speaks some of the language from school coursework
A translation app the patient can use alone once the visit ends

explanation: Postoperative instructions need a qualified interpreter under facility policy so clinical meaning is not edited or guessed. School language study, a phone app, and a volunteering relative are not the same as medical interpreting.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an adult relative with a qualified interpreter; a daughter may omit, add, or soften instructions and hear details the patient did not choose to share.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coursework with medical interpreting; a billing coworker can mistranslate clinical terms even when the everyday language sounds familiar.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses machine translation with language access; an app is unreliable for postoperative directions the patient must follow.

prompt: A patient offers the CMAA free bookkeeping from the patient's company and asks for a personal cell number for faster scheduling. A friend also wants the CMAA to open that friend's chart. Which stance is professional?

options.text: Give the personal cell number so scheduling requests can move faster
Keep a respectful, non-exploitative relationship and decline the offers
Accept the free bookkeeping as a thank-you between people who know each other
Open the friend's chart and read the new results aloud as a favor

explanation: Administrative staff keep a respectful relationship that does not exploit the patient or the CMAA. A personal number, free services from a patient's business, and opening a friend's chart each turn the job into a private favor.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses convenience with boundaries; a personal cell number bypasses documented office scheduling channels.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a thank-you with a second relationship; free bookkeeping creates a debt and a dual relationship with a patient.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses friendship with a job need; opening a friend's chart without a work reason is a privacy breach, and reading results is outside the CMAA role.

prompt: While scheduling a follow-up, an older patient whispers that a caregiver withholds food when the patient complains. The caregiver is sitting in the lobby. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Follow the office abuse-reporting steps and alert a supervisor
Ask the caregiver in the lobby to explain the feeding comment right then
Set the whisper aside because scheduling staff are not the treating clinicians
Promise the patient the comment will stay between the two of you

explanation: A report of withheld food is suspected neglect, and the CMAA starts the practice's reporting steps, including telling a supervisor or the designated reporter. The front desk does not investigate the caregiver in public or promise to keep the report secret.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses reporting with investigating; confronting the caregiver in the lobby can endanger the patient and is outside the CMAA role.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses clinical licensure with the duty to pass on suspected neglect; administrative staff still start the office reporting steps.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses confidentiality toward the caregiver with secrecy from the reporting path; a personal promise conflicts with the abuse-reporting policy.

prompt: A patient calls and asks the CMAA whether to stop a blood-pressure pill after reading about side effects online. The physician is with another patient. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Decline to advise and route the question to the physician or clinical staff
Suggest holding the pill until the physician can return the call tomorrow
Read the package insert aloud and say the current dose is safe to keep
Tell the patient the article is mistaken and the present dose should continue

explanation: Starting, stopping, or endorsing a medication is a clinical decision. The CMAA does not make that call from an online article or a package insert. The safe step is to connect the patient with the physician or another clinician who can advise.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a holding suggestion with a message; telling the patient to stop the pill until tomorrow is medication advice outside the CMAA scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses reading an insert with authority to judge safety; calling the dose safe is a clinical conclusion the front desk cannot make.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses reassurance with scope; rejecting the article and locking in the dose is still medical advice.

prompt: A durable-equipment representative offers the CMAA a catered lunch each month if the desk starts recommending that company's brace to patients. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Decline the lunches and report the offer under the compliance policy
Accept the monthly lunch if that brace is sometimes medically useful for patients
Split the lunches across the front desk so no one person receives the whole gift
Agree to recommend the brace but leave the lunch deal out of any written record

explanation: Meals given so staff will steer patients to one product are a referral inducement. Whether the brace is sometimes appropriate does not make the personal benefit acceptable. The CMAA refuses the offer and puts it on the compliance path.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses clinical usefulness with a clean referral; a lunch conditioned on recommendations is the inducement, even if the product sometimes fits.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses sharing a gift with refusing it; splitting the meals still ties a personal benefit to steering patients.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses secrecy with compliance; hiding the arrangement skips the review that exists to catch vendor inducements.

prompt: A coworker asks the CMAA to change the authorization date so an imaging claim looks as if it was authorized before the scan. The authorization actually arrived the next day. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Refuse the date change and report the request through the compliance channel
Enter the earlier date because the authorization did arrive the following morning
Change the date in the note and keep the original form in a side folder
Make the edit if the coworker says the payer is unlikely to compare the dates

explanation: Changing the authorization date so the approval appears to have come before the scan creates a false record in support of a claim. The CMAA refuses the edit and reports the request through compliance instead of helping the file show the wrong sequence.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses later approval with an earlier date; arrival the next day does not justify pretending the approval came before the scan.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses hiding the original with an honest record; a note that shows the wrong date is still a false timeline.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses audit odds with truthfulness; a date the CMAA knows is wrong falsifies the record whether or not a payer looks.

prompt: When a deaf patient arrives for a new-patient visit and asks to communicate in American Sign Language, a teenage child offers to sign. What should the CMAA arrange?

options.text: Handwritten notes, so registration can begin without waiting
The teenage child, who already signs with the patient at home
A qualified sign-language interpreter under facility policy
Louder speech and gestures, because this stop is just check-in

explanation: A deaf patient who asks for American Sign Language at a new-patient visit should receive a qualified interpreter under facility policy. A child who signs at home, passed notes, or louder speech does not provide that effective communication for a full visit.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses brief written notes with the requested language; paper can support a short exchange but does not replace sign language for this visit.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a family signer with a qualified interpreter; a teenager may omit information the patient needs at registration.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses volume with access; louder speech and gestures assume hearing and ignore the sign language the patient requested.

prompt: A law-office clerk hands the CMAA a subpoena for a patient's chart and asks for copies before leaving the lobby. The patient has not signed a release. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Copy the chart immediately, because a subpoena stands in for the patient's signature
Refuse the papers and tell the clerk to return after the patient signs a release
Accept the subpoena and follow the practice's legal-release process before any copies go out
Release the latest visit notes if the clerk shows a business card from the firm

explanation: A subpoena is a legal demand the front desk should accept and route, not a reason to hand over the chart in the lobby and not a document to turn away. Privacy or legal staff follow the practice process to decide what may be disclosed and when.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a subpoena with instant authority for the CMAA; same-minute copying skips the practice review of what the demand actually requires.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a missing patient signature with a reason to reject service; the papers should be accepted and routed, not sent back to the lobby door.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a business card with authority to receive PHI; visit notes are still a disclosure and still go through the release process.

prompt: A patient brings a signed healthcare proxy and asks the CMAA whether the named agent may decide about today's lab work. What should the CMAA do with the form?

options.text: Rule that the agent may approve today's labs and write that decision in the note
Hand the form back, because an attorney has to place it in the medical record
File the form in the chart and alert the clinical team without interpreting it
Type the agent's name into the appointment note and shred the signed original

explanation: The CMAA files a healthcare proxy the patient brings and makes sure the clinical team knows it is in the record. Deciding whether the agent controls today's labs interprets the document, which is a clinical and legal judgment, not a front-desk ruling.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses filing with interpretation; declaring that the agent controls today's labs decides a question the CMAA is not authorized to decide.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses legal advice with filing; a patient may give the practice the proxy, and an attorney is not required to place that copy in the chart.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a typed name with the document; shredding the original removes the form clinicians need to read.

prompt: A specialist's office calls with a question about a patient's diagnosis while the CMAA is checking in a line of people at the open counter. How should the CMAA handle the call?

options.text: Discuss the diagnosis at the counter so the specialist's staff are not kept waiting
Switch the call to speaker so a coworker can confirm the spelling of the diagnosis
Move to a private area before saying anything about the diagnosis
Ask the patients in line to step outside and continue the call at the same counter

explanation: Diagnosis details are protected information, and an open check-in line can overhear a counter conversation or a speaker call. The CMAA moves to a private spot before discussing the case. Sending the line outside does not make the counter private.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses courtesy to the caller with privacy; speed does not outweigh people standing within earshot of the diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a spelling check with a private call; speakerphone at the desk broadcasts the diagnosis to the line.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an emptied lobby with a private workspace; an open counter is still not the place to discuss the diagnosis.

prompt: A patient says the practice discriminated during scheduling and wants the complaint on record. The CMAA believes the schedule that day was fair. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Tell the patient that discrimination complaints must be submitted by an attorney first
Decline to log the complaint because the schedule looked fair from the desk
Explain how to file a grievance and accept the complaint as policy directs
Suggest posting the story on a public review site instead of an internal form

explanation: A patient's right to file a grievance does not depend on whether the CMAA thinks the schedule was fair. The CMAA explains the practice process and accepts the complaint. Blocking it, requiring a lawyer first, or pointing the patient to a public post skips that process.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a lawsuit with an internal grievance; an attorney is not required before the practice will receive a discrimination complaint.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the CMAA's impression with the patient's right; thinking the schedule looked fair does not erase the duty to log the complaint.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a public review with the grievance path; the practice is supposed to offer its own complaint process.

prompt: A coworker posts a waiting-room photo that shows a patient's distinctive tattoo and the practice name, then says no names were used. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Leave the post up, because a photo without a printed name is anonymous
Comment with the patient's first name so friends can send get-well wishes
Repost a cropped copy on the practice page if most of the tattoo is cut out
Ask that the post come down and report it under the privacy policy

explanation: A waiting-room image that shows a distinctive tattoo together with the practice name can identify a patient even when no name is written on the post. The CMAA asks for removal and reports the disclosure under the privacy policy rather than spreading the image further.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a missing name with anonymity; a unique tattoo in a named clinic's waiting room can still identify the patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses well-wishes with privacy; adding a name increases the disclosure instead of stopping it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses cropping with a fix; reposting from the practice account spreads a patient image and leaves the original post up.

prompt: At the entrance, a patient with a dog states that the dog is a service animal for a disability. Another patient asks the CMAA to make the dog wait outside. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Demand written proof of the disability before the dog may come into the office
Refuse the dog because the other patient prefers that animals stay outside
Allow the dog if the patient first pays an added cleaning charge
Allow the dog in patient areas and skip demands for proof of the disability

explanation: When a patient states that a dog is a service animal, the dog is allowed in patient areas. Staff do not demand documentation of the disability, charge a pet-style cleaning fee, or remove the dog because another patient objects. If the task is unclear, the permitted questions are whether the dog is required because of a disability and what task it performs.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a service animal with a pet that needs papers; demanding proof of the disability goes past the questions staff may ask.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses another patient's preference with access rules; an objection does not override the handler's right to bring the service animal in.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a service animal with a pet boarding fee; a cleaning surcharge treats the dog as a pet rather than as an access aid.

prompt: During a scheduling call, a patient describes crushing chest pressure and shortness of breath and then asks for the next routine opening. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Offer the next routine opening later in the week and ask the patient to wait
Say the pressure is probably heartburn and place the patient on the regular schedule
Ask the patient to drive in whenever a gap shows up on the book
Follow the office emergency protocol instead of booking a routine slot

explanation: Crushing chest pressure with shortness of breath is an emergency presentation, not a request for an ordinary future visit. The CMAA follows the practice emergency steps so clinical or emergency help starts now, rather than offering a later routine appointment.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a routine book with an emergency; a later ordinary opening delays help for chest pressure and shortness of breath.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a front-desk guess with assessment; naming heartburn is a clinical judgment the CMAA must not make on this call.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coming in for a gap with emergency handling; driving over when the book loosens still treats the call as ordinary scheduling.

prompt: Before a sensitive exam, a patient asks for a clinician of the same gender and explains that the request matches their cultural practice. A same-gender clinician is free that day. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Tell the patient that cultural preferences are not part of the scheduling process
Keep the assigned clinician so the appointment book does not have to be reworked
Cancel the exam because the practice does not rearrange staff for gender requests
Offer the available same-gender clinician and record the request in the schedule

explanation: When a same-gender clinician is available, a cultural modesty request is a scheduling preference the desk can honor. The CMAA offers that clinician and records the request so the visit matches what the patient asked for, instead of refusing or cancelling.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a cultural modesty need with an irrelevant preference; the schedule can already meet the request the same day.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses schedule convenience with respect; keeping the assigned clinician overrides a preference the practice can honor.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses accommodation with cancellation; ending the exam punishes a request that an available clinician can meet.

prompt: The CMAA notices staff routinely erase copays for every patient as a courtesy, with no hardship review and no note in the record. A coworker says everyone does it. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Keep waiving the copays so patients are not upset when they reach checkout
Waive the copay for patients who already know they can ask for the courtesy
Post the copay and then delete it so the ledger still looks as if it was collected
Stop participating and report the routine waiver pattern through compliance

explanation: Erasing copays for every patient, with no hardship process and no record, is a compliance concern because routine forgiveness can be a beneficiary inducement. The CMAA should not continue the pattern or disguise it. The pattern belongs on the compliance reporting path.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses checkout satisfaction with a compliant waiver; a standing courtesy for every patient skips any hardship review.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a quieter version of the same practice with a fix; limiting the waiver to people who know to ask still skips a hardship process.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a tidy ledger with an honest one; posting and then deleting the copay falsifies what was collected.

prompt: A 16-year-old patient asks the CMAA to keep today's visit off any statement a parent could see and not to mention the visit if a parent calls. What should the CMAA do?

options.text: Promise complete secrecy and block every parent inquiry about today's visit
Call the parent immediately and describe the reason the teen came in
Tell the teen the front desk can hide any visit whenever a minor asks
Follow the practice minor-privacy policy and involve a supervisor or clinician

explanation: Whether a parent may see a minor's visit depends on the service and on rules that are not the same everywhere. The CMAA does not invent a blanket promise or an automatic parent call. The practice minor-privacy policy, with a supervisor or clinician, decides what may be shared.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a teen's request with a promise the desk can keep; total secrecy can conflict with policy and with notices a parent may be entitled to receive.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses parental involvement with automatic disclosure; describing the reason for the visit can reveal information the policy may protect.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses front-desk discretion with policy; the CMAA does not have a free-standing power to hide every minor visit on request.
